title: From Bakery Shifts to Seven-Figure Revenue: One Indian Founder's Australian Climb
excerpt: Yatin Jindal arrived in Australia at 18 with no network and worked bakery, convenience-store and security shifts. Four years after founding Digital Route, he says the agency has served 50-plus property professionals and driven $12.5 million in client revenue.
body:
• Yatin Jindal arrived in Australia at 18 with no professional network, working bakery, convenience-store and security shifts before founding the Melbourne marketing agency Digital Route in 2022.
  • His first break came from a late-night conversation at Thomastown station with a solar-company contact — a $300-a-month contract that grew to $2,500 a month within six months.
  • The agency's measurement-first model links ads, landing pages, lead qualification, follow-up and revenue reporting; it claims 15x revenue growth on one property campaign and 50-plus qualified enquiries a week on another.
  • Four years on, the company says it has served more than 50 property professionals and helped generate over $12.5 million in combined client revenue, with clients in Australia plus engagements in Dubai and Singapore.

At 18, Yatin Jindal left India for Australia without an established professional network. Before he started a business, he took shifts in a bakery, a convenience store and security work to keep himself afloat. He built his first company around those working hours. Four years later, his Melbourne-based agency Digital Route says it has worked with more than 50 property professionals and helped generate over $12.5 million in combined client revenue — a climb from shift work to a seven-figure business, by the company's own account.

The first break

Digital Route was founded in Australia in 2022, based in Epping, Victoria. The turning point, according to the founder's account, was unglamorous: a late-night conversation at Thomastown station with someone connected to a solar company. That conversation led to a contract worth about $300 a month. Within six months, as the work expanded, the engagement had grown to roughly $2,500 a month — the wedge that let Jindal leave shift work behind and invest full-time in the agency.

A method, not just ads

The early contract shaped how the agency approached later campaigns. Rather than treating an advertisement as the complete job, the team began connecting the advertisement, landing page, lead qualification, follow-up and revenue reporting into a single system. Performance was judged by qualified enquiries, booked appointments, conversions and attributable revenue rather than clicks and impressions alone.

"The first contract was small, but it forced me to understand every part of the process: finding an opportunity, making the offer, delivering the work and giving the client a reason to stay."

— Yatin Jindal, founder of Digital Route

Jindal's account of the lesson is direct: advertising alone was not enough, and the landing page, lead quality, follow-up and sales process had to work together. It is a deliberate positioning in a crowded performance-marketing market, where many agencies report on traffic while clients care about revenue.

The numbers

Four years after the journey began, the company's reported results include 15x revenue growth over six months for one property campaign, more than 50 qualified enquiries a week for another, and a 28% improvement in return on ad spend on the same campaign. The agency says it has helped more than 60 property professionals generate over $12.5 million in combined revenue — figures that are company-reported and refer to client revenue rather than the agency's own books, a distinction worth keeping straight.

Digital Route remains based in Epping, Victoria. Its work has centred on property professionals and service businesses across Australia, alongside international engagements in Dubai and Singapore. As a performance-marketing and web-development agency, it connects Google Ads, Meta Ads, conversion-focused websites, lead qualification, CRM automation and reporting into measurable lead-generation systems.

Diaspora Angle

The story fits a familiar arc in the Indian diaspora: the migrant who arrives young, works whatever jobs pay, and builds a business from the ground up. What distinguishes Jindal's case is the niche — Australian property marketing, a high-ticket, referral-heavy sector where an outsider with no network might seem least likely to break in. His answer was to make results the network: measurable revenue, tracked from ad click to closed deal, that sells itself to the next client. For young Indian migrants weighing entrepreneurship against the safety of a salary, it is a reminder that the riskiest part of starting is often simply starting.

What's Next

Digital Route continues to work with property professionals, service businesses and growing companies across Australia, with its Dubai and Singapore engagements pointing to an international footprint. Whether the agency's self-reported seven-figure trajectory sustains in a more crowded market will depend on the same thing that started it: the willingness to be judged on revenue, not impressions.
